extracted.intended_audience: NLP / computational-linguistics and machine-learning researchers interested in computational humor recognition
extracted.subtask_description: Automatic recognition of verbally expressed humor restricted to one-liners (short single-sentence jokes). The task is framed as a supervised text classification problem using stylistic heuristics, content features, and ensemble methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-liner selection (positive examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-liner is a short sentence with comic effects and an interesting linguistic structure: simple syntax, deliberate use of rhetoric devices (e.g. alliteration, rhyme), and frequent use of creative language constructions meant to attract the reader's attention. Usually 15 or less words; produces the humorous effect 'in one shot'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one-sentence jokes (typically ≤15 words) as positive training data; examples provided (e.g. 'Take my advice; I don’t use it anyway.'). One-liners are chosen because humor-producing features are guaranteed to be present in the single sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web-based bootstrapping — thematic constraint (URL keywords)
rubrics_metrics.description: When bootstrapping one-liners from the Web, require that at least one keyword indicating humor-related content appears in the URL of a retrieved webpage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implementation used a small set of keywords (oneliner, one-liner, humor, humour, joke, funny) to bias retrieved pages toward humor-related content (e.g. http://www.berro.com/Jokes). This helps steer the bootstrap away from noisy, non-humor pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web-based bootstrapping — structural constraint (HTML enumerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit HTML structure (enumerations) to find pages where seed one-liners appear in lists; other items in the same enumeration are likely to be one-liners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect HTML list tags (e.g. <li>) and extract candidate lines in the same enumeration as a seed one-liner. Assumes enumerations include texts of similar genre; repeat iterations to expand seed set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate removal / string-similarity filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove duplicate or near-duplicate entries using a string-similarity measure based on longest common subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice two iterations of bootstrapping produced ~24,000 candidates; duplicate removal left ~16,000 distinct one-liners. Manual verification on a sample indicates ~9% noise remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative data selection: structurally and stylistically similar negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Select negative examples that are non-humorous but similar in structure and style to one-liners so classifiers cannot rely on trivial cues like length or obvious vocabulary differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper used three negative sets: (1) Reuters news titles, (2) Proverbs from online collections, (3) BNC sentences selected to be content-similar. This forces models to learn humor-specific features rather than surface differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length restriction for positives and negatives (10–15 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforce the same length restriction on negative examples as on one-liners: one sentence, average length 10–15 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeps structural and stylistic properties comparable between classes to avoid confounding classification by length.

rubrics_metrics.name: BNC negative selection via IR (tf.idf + cosine similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select BNC sentences most similar to each one-liner using an information retrieval approach: tf.idf weighting and cosine similarity (SMART system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An index of BNC sentences of length 10–15 words is used; the most similar sentence to each one-liner is retrieved and used as a negative example to ensure topical similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic feature — Alliteration/rhyme chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the number of alliteration/rhyme chains in each sentence as an indicator of stylistic humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alliteration and phonetic devices are important; extraction used an index built on top of the CMU pronunciation dictionary. Alliteration was found to be the most useful single stylistic indicator in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic feature — Antonymy (semantic opposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect presence of antonyms in a sentence using WordNet antonymy relations (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) and indirect antonymy via 'similar-to' for adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonymy is a proxy for incongruity/opposition. Coverage is limited by WordNet; deeper semantic analysis (word-sense/domain disambiguation) could improve detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic feature — Adult slang (sexuality domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect sexual-oriented lexicon by extracting synsets labeled with the domain SEXUALITY from WordNet Domains, remove highly polysemous words, and check presence in sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for humor based on adult slang; WordNet Domains coverage is incomplete and highly polysemous words are filtered out to reduce noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic application & thresholding for stylistic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat stylistic features (alliteration, antonymy, adult slang) as numerical heuristics requiring a threshold to decide humorous vs non-humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds are learned automatically using a decision tree on a small labeled subset (1000 examples); apply learned threshold to remaining data. These features act as heuristics rather than features that always improve with more data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based features and classifiers (bag-of-words / tf.idf; Naive Bayes and SVM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate humor-recognition as a text classification task using content-based features (e.g., tf.idf weighted word features) and standard classifiers: multinomial Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naive Bayes (multinomial) and SVM were chosen for prior strong performance and methodological diversity. Reported accuracies: Naive Bayes and SVM achieve substantially higher accuracy than stylistic heuristics in most settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature combination via stacked learner (ensemble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine content-based classifier output with stylistic features in a stacked learning framework: feed text-classifier output + stylistic features into a memory-based learner (Timbl).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a memory-based learner in the second stage to avoid discarding low-performance but informative stylistic features; using a decision tree in the second stage led to ignoring stylistic features in favor of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation protocol: stratified ten-fold cross-validation and baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate models with stratified ten-fold cross-validation. Use appropriate baselines: 50% for balanced class distributions and 75% when using 75/25 negative/positive splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report accuracy and perform statistical significance testing (paired t-test) when comparing methods. Also examine performance under uneven class distributions to reflect harder settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary performance metrics: classification accuracy and learning curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Use classification accuracy as the main performance metric and plot learning curves (accuracy vs fraction of training data) to study learning behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning curves reveal how accuracy improves with data size; the paper observed significant learning up to ~60% of the data (~10,000 positive examples) and a plateau/drop beyond that, suggesting more sophisticated features are needed rather than simply more data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple negative sets and mixed negatives to test bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use diverse negative sets (Reuters titles, proverbs, BNC sentences) and also a mixed negative set to ensure reported results are not biased by a particular negative collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments across multiple negative types help verify that classifiers learn humor-specific features rather than artifacts of a single negative source; comparable results on mixed negatives validate robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual verification and acceptable noise level
rubrics_metrics.description: Manually inspect a sample of automatically collected positive examples to estimate noise; in the paper a random sample of 200 one-liners indicated ~9% potential noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept some level of noise from automatic collection; be aware noise may explain learning curve plateaus for very large data sets. Report and consider noise in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature analysis for future feature engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze learned content features to discover useful indicators (e.g., frequent human-related words and negative word forms in one-liners), and use these observations to guide future feature development (semantic opposition, ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect top content features from classifiers to identify patterns (references to man/woman/person/you/I; negative verb/adjective forms). Use such analyses to propose new humor-specific semantic or pragmatic features for improved recognition.
